question: Every year, thousands of women in the EU lose their lives because of their gender. Femicide is the most extreme form of gender-based violence. In the EU, the available data on femicide comes primarily from general homicide statistics, which mainly allow the identification of femicide committed by intimate partners or family members.

Femicide committed outside intimate and family relationships is therefore ignored, which leads to an underestimation and downgrading of the true extent of the phenomenon.1 Most Member States have not legally recognised the term ‘femicide’, which makes it difficult to measure and makes it ‘invisible’ in general homicide statistics.
2 At the same time, there is still a lack of standardised methods for collecting and categorising the relevant data.

3 Given that: - EIGE has repeatedly called for a common definition of femicide4 as a basis for reliable data, effective policies and recognition of the gender dimension of violence, - Article 44 of Directive 2024/1385 states that Member States must cooperate with EIGE in collecting comparable data on violence against women, the following questions arise: 1.
Does the Council intend to include the issue of femicide in its work priorities?

How does the Council intend to contribute, within its remit, to the promotion of a common European definition of femicide among Member States and to the coordination of cooperation with EIGE on the implementation of harmonised data collection standards, in accordance with Directive 2024/1385?

For example, femicide committed against women working in the sex trade or other vulnerable groups is not taken into account. Only five out of 27 Member States have legally recognised the term ‘femicide’. The lack of a single definition leads to incomplete and incomparable statistics, while different legal approaches in Member States lead to inconsistencies in addressing the problem.

The systematic collection of national and regional administrative data is essential to understanding the true extent of the phenomenon in Member States. Furthermore, it helps to identify high-risk groups and to develop targeted laws and policies to address the root causes of femicide, ensuring that these cases are effectively investigated and prosecuted.
EIGE defines ‘femicide’ as the killing of women and girls because of their gender (https://eige.europa.eu/publications-resources/thesaurus/terms/1192?language_content_entity=en).
answer: Further to the adoption of Directive (EU) 2024/1385, the Council reaffirmed its commitment in its conclusions of 17 October 2025 on ‘violence against women and domestic violence: prevention, early detection and intervention’1, explicitly noting that women and girls are disproportionately exposed to gender-based violence, including its most extreme and brutal manifestations such as femicide.
Article 44 of Directive (EU) 2024/1385 provides for obligations in relation to data collection and research.

In order to ensure the comparability and standardisation of administrative data across the Union, Member States must endeavour to collect administrative data on the basis of common disaggregations developed in cooperation with and in accordance with the standards developed by the European Institute for Gender Equality (EIGE). The deadline for the transposition of the Directive is 14 June 2027.

In its abovementioned Council conclusions, the Council called on the European Commission and the Member States to improve the data collection, analysis, publication and use of data on violence against women and domestic violence.

In the framework of the Council of Europe Convention on preventing and combating violence against women and domestic violence (‘Istanbul Convention’), a thematic discussion on preventing and combating gender-related killings/femicide was held at the Committee of the Parties’ meeting on 11 December 2025.
As the Union is a party to the Convention, it participated in the discussion and the Commission debriefed the Council’s competent working party on the outcome.
